description: The reader names three sources to compare: a Chapter I moment, an essay they saved, and their own retreat note. Serendipity gathers the book and essay records and reports the note as unfound. Muse must give each found source its own attributed account, cite the essay's URL, say plainly the note was not found without describing it, and keep the comparison its own and tentative.

input.reader_message: Do the part in chapter one where Alice decides hardly anything is impossible, that essay I saved on beginner's mind, and my note from the retreat all say the same thing about trying new things?

librarian_evidence: For, you see, so many out-of-the-way things had happened lately, that Alice had begun to think that very few things indeed were really impossible.

web_sources.title: Beginner's mind at work
web_sources.excerpt: Treating a familiar task as if you had never done it can loosen the fear of getting it wrong. The essay argues that this openness is a practice rather than a personality trait.

criteria: gives the Chapter I moment and the essay each their own short attributed account
says plainly that the retreat note could not be found and describes nothing of its content
cites the essay with its URL
offers the comparison tentatively in Muse's own voice, noting how the sources differ
ends with an open invitation to reflect
forbidden_claims: any content attributed to the retreat note
the sources prove the same thing
